5	
6	# @deepseek-ai/dsh-workspace
7	
8	## Summary
9	
10	`dsh-workspace` gives a host a persistent set of workspaces: named user directories, each with the sessions that ran in it, kept in a stable order across restarts. With it, a UI can show a sidebar of projects, attach sessions to the right project, hide a session from the grouping without losing it, and remove a project — removal never deletes the folder or the session histories, which become ungrouped. Use it in GUI or host compositions that need durable project grouping; headless and minimal runs can omit it entirely. The package is host-side only: the model, tools, and agent loop never see it, so it adds no tokens, prompts, or request context. It needs a session store and a persistence backend mounted alongside it; setup is a few composition rows.

23	<a id="use-this-package"></a>
24	## Use this package
25	
26	Use this package to give the product a project list: named directories the user works in, the sessions that ran in each, a stable order, and a way to hide sessions without losing them. The API contracts behind each action live in the implementation section.
27	
28	### When to use it
29	
30	Use it when the product shows a persistent workspace surface — a sidebar, session grouping, or automation that names directories and orders them. It is invisible to the model, so it adds no token or request cost. Skip it when there is no grouping surface; nothing else in the harness needs it.
31	
32	### Setting up
33	
34	The package takes no configuration of its own; it needs a session store, a session persistence backend, and the storage rows that keep its records. A minimal composition:
35	
36	```yaml
37	- name: '@deepseek-ai/dsh-session'
38	- name: '@deepseek-ai/dsh-session-persistence-jsonl'
39	- name: '@deepseek-ai/dsh-storage'
40	- name: '@deepseek-ai/dsh-storage-json'
41	- name: '@deepseek-ai/dsh-storage-domain'
42	  config:
43	    backend: json
44	- name: '@deepseek-ai/dsh-workspace'
45	```
46	
47	With these rows mounted, creating a project shows up in the list immediately and survives a restart; the first start also groups existing sessions by the directory they ran in. If a required peer is missing, the workspace feature stays unavailable until it is mounted.

6	# @deepseek-ai/dsh-agent-instructions
7	
8	## Summary
9	
10	`dsh-agent-instructions` loads `AGENTS.md`-compatible workspace instruction files into model context: the user-global file and the project chain reach the first request as one durable baseline, and successful `read`, `write`, or `edit` calls bring newly relevant nested files, changes, and removals into later requests. `dsh-base` includes it by default, and a profile patch can disable it. Everything is bounded by a byte budget: broader files are omitted before the most specific file is truncated, and an empty chain contributes nothing. There is no file watcher — external edits become visible on the next successful filesystem touch or when a resumed session reconciles its baseline.

23	<a id="use-this-package"></a>
24	## Use this package
25	
26	Mount this plugin when agents should work from the workspace's own instruction files. `dsh-base` already includes it with a 65,536-byte budget, so base-backed profiles only need to replace the row when they want another `maxBytes`; providerless trees load nothing until a filesystem provider is present.
27	
28	### What the agent gets
29	
30	The first request includes one durable baseline message with the user-global `$DSH_HOME/AGENTS.md` followed by the project chain — every existing candidate file from the project root down to the session working directory, in broad-to-specific order. Sibling files whose content matches after trimming render once, so a `CLAUDE.md` that duplicates its `AGENTS.md` is not repeated. After a successful `read`, `write`, or `edit` call reaches a deeper directory, the next request includes the newly applicable instruction file; a changed file replaces its content, and a file that disappears or duplicates an earlier candidate produces a removal notice.
31	
32	### Configuration
33	
34	The defaults suit a typical checkout: `.git` marks the project root, `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` are the base candidates, and `AGENTS.local.md` and `CLAUDE.local.md` are additive local overlays. Only `maxBytes` is required — it caps the complete rendered baseline so each deployment chooses its prompt budget explicitly.
35	
36	```yaml
37	- name: '@deepseek-ai/dsh-agent-instructions'
38	  config:
39	    maxBytes: 65536
40	```
````

Each call runs ripgrep itself with a fixed argument set and returns workdir-relative results, and the tools are always available because every carrier packages ripgrep. 25

27

29	
30	A subprocess backend, then the tools; the spill backend is optional and makes capped results fully recoverable.

34	- name: '@deepseek-ai/dsh-tool-fs-search'
35	  config:
36	    sampleOverCapGlobResults: false
37	- name: '@deepseek-ai/dsh-spill-local'
38	```
39	
40	`sampleOverCapGlobResults` is required and has no fallback: deployments choose the over-cap ordering contract explicitly. When formatted spill succeeds, both modes preserve the complete sorted list in the spill artifact.

No. This harness does **no indexing of the codebase**: no embeddings, no vector store, no repo map, no startup file scan. A folder with a codebase and an empty folder are handled the same way. The only difference is what the agent finds when it looks.

**What reaches the model on the first request (both cases):**
- **The system prompt** (`snapshots/web/ptc-round/system-prompt.expected.md`). It gives the working directory as a plain path and describes the tools. It includes no file listing or code summary.
- **Instruction files**, via `packages/context/agent-instructions`. It loads `$DSH_HOME/AGENTS.md` plus any `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` found from the project root (marked by `.git`) down to the working directory, up to 64 KB (`maxBytes: 65536`). In an empty folder there are none, so nothing is added. This is the only codebase-specific content injected automatically, and it is file loading, not indexing.

**How the agent learns the codebase: on demand, one query at a time.**
- `glob` and `grep` (`packages/fs/tool-fs-search`) run a bundled ripgrep against the live filesystem on every call. Nothing is precomputed or cached.
- `read`, `bash`, and subagents are the other ways it explores. In an empty folder these return nothing, and the agent just starts creating files.
- When a `read`/`write`/`edit` reaches a deeper directory, any nested `AGENTS.md` there gets added to later requests. That is still lazy, not a scan.

**Two things that look like indexing but aren't codebase indexing:**
- `dsh-workspace` keeps a "header index" of **sessions**: which chat sessions ran in which project folder, for the sidebar. It reads session headers only. It never reads your code, and its README says the model never sees any of it.
- `session-query-sqlite` is full-text search over **past session logs**, not code. It also ships turned off (`openAt: never` in both `packages/bundle/base/cordis.patch.yml` and `packages/bundle/web-app/cordis.patch.yml`).

If you want real codebase indexing (a repo map or semantic search), it would go in as a new context or tool plugin rather than a change to `agent-loop`, per the "Plugins, not loop changes" rule in AGENTS.md.

55	## Understand the implementation
56	
57	<details>
58	<summary>Implementation internals — click to expand</summary>
59	
60	This section explains the design of the provider; the observable behavior is covered in [Use this package](#use-this-package).
61	
62	### Design concept
63	
64	The provider maintains one reusable `WorkspaceFileSearch` per agent, rooted at that session's `cwd`. Directory-scoped queries (`a/b/...`) list live directory state, while bare fuzzy queries share one bounded recursive traversal. Only a workspace's first bare query waits for that traversal; a `tool/result` event marks the settled entries stale, and the next bare query serves them while the replacement builds. The model guidance is a per-agent prompt section contributed only while the addressed agent has a `read` tool; agent disposal releases both the index and the prompt fiber.
65	
66	### Source map
67	
68	| File | Role |
69	|---|---|
70	| [`src/index.ts`](src/index.ts) | `LocalFileReferenceService`: config validation, per-agent searches, prompt install |
71	| [`src/search.ts`](src/search.ts) | `WorkspaceFileSearch`: traversal, ranking, exclusion, staleness and background rebuild |
72	| [`src/invariant.ts`](src/invariant.ts) | Invariant companion for the discovery contract |
73	
74	### Main flow
75	
76	A `list(agent, query, signal)` call either lists one directory's entries or reads the shared bounded index, ranks the candidates (exact, prefix, substring, then subsequence scores with directory bonuses), and returns at most `maxResults` in deterministic order. `tool/result` events mark the addressed agent's index stale so a later bare query observes a fresh tree. An unreadable or excluded subtree contributes no candidates, while an unreadable root fails its traversal instead: a transient failure must not replace still-good entries with an empty index.
77	
78	</details>

No, and my first answer had a mistake. There **is** one index I missed, but it isn't the kind you probably mean.

**The correction: an `@file` autocomplete index.** `packages/context/file-reference-local` ships in the default web profile (`packages/bundle/web-app/cordis.patch.yml:72`). It builds a list of file and directory paths in the working directory:
- It stores **paths only**, not file contents. It holds up to 50,000 entries and skips `.git`, `node_modules`, `dist`, `build` and similar folders.
- **It is built lazily.** Nothing is scanned when a session starts or when you send a query. The traversal runs the first time you type `@` plus a bare name in the chat box (`search.ts:159-161`).
- After any tool call it is marked stale and rebuilt in the background the next time you use `@`.
- **The model never sees it.** It only powers the autocomplete dropdown. The only thing it adds to the model's context is one fixed sentence in the system prompt explaining what `@path` means.

**So for your two cases:**
- **Folder with a codebase:** nothing is indexed when a query arrives. The model gets the system prompt, plus any `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` files. It then explores with `glob`/`grep`/`read`, which run live ripgrep searches each time. If you use `@` autocomplete, a path list gets built for the dropdown.
- **Empty folder:** the same pipeline runs. No instruction files are found, and the path list, if built, is empty.

**How sure I am now.** I searched the source of every package and app for embeddings, vector stores, tree-sitter, ctags, repo maps, file watchers and recursive directory walks. Apart from the `@file` path list, nothing indexes your code:
- The three file watchers I found watch only the credentials file, the settings file and skill folders.
- The only "embeddings" mention is Exa's web search provider, which works on the web, not your code.

I haven't traced every plugin at runtime, so I won't say 100%. But from the source I read, the model gets no semantic, symbol or content index of your code.

`dsh-session-title-llm` runs model-backed title generation through one shared policy: it resolves the auxiliary route, frames the exact selected human messages as JSON, enforces input and output budgets, composes timeout and caller cancellation, and validates the model's output before a title is accepted. It is a library, not a Cordis plugin — the shipped provider plugins call `registerSessionTitleLlmProvider()` with their cadence and message selector, and the helper validates shared config and delegates every revision to one generation path, so registration, route, prompt, cancellation, and validation behavior cannot drift between them. Deployments configure it through the provider plugins, which require every limit. The route, failure, and configuration contracts come first; the request internals live in a collapsible developer section below.

No. The harness has no query classifier agent. Your message goes straight to the one main agent (`packages/core/agent-loop`) with no model call, routing step or intent check before it.

**Every LLM call the harness makes:**
- **The main agent loop:** the actual answer to your query.
- **Session titles** (`packages/session/session-title-llm`): a side call that reads your messages and writes a title for the sidebar. It runs alongside the conversation and doesn't change how the query is handled.
- **Compaction** (`packages/compaction/compaction-basic/src/summarizer.ts`): summarizes old history when the context gets too long. It isn't triggered by a new query.

**Things that look like classification but aren't:**
- **Choosing the model** (`packages/core/agent/src/model-selection.ts`) just uses whatever provider and model are selected in the UI. Nothing looks at your query to pick one.
- **Tool-call "classify"** (`packages/core/tools/src/ptc.ts`, `agent-loop/src/tool-calls.ts`) decides whether the model's tool calls can run in parallel or one at a time. It never sees your query.
- **Session `origin: 'subagent'`** is a label marking a session as a child of another session, used for display.

**Where the "classifying" actually happens:** inside the main model, guided by its system prompt. The prompt tells it when to create a goal ("may infer goal intent from a direct human request"), when to use a workflow, Ralph loop or subagent, and when to load a skill. So the one agent decides for itself how to handle each query. There's no separate agent in front of it.

I confirmed this by searching the source of every package for classifier or intent code and for every place that makes an LLM call. If you wanted a real router, the way this repo is built it would be a new plugin, not a change to `agent-loop`.

No. The harness does no graph, semantic or lexical indexing of the user's codebase. The only lexical index is for past chat sessions, and it ships switched off. The only graphs are build-time tools for the harness's own source.

**Semantic: none.** No embeddings, vector store or similarity search exists anywhere in the source. The only "embeddings" mention is Exa's web search provider, which searches the web, not your code.

**Lexical: one index, and it covers chats, not code.**
- **What it is:** `packages/session-query/session-query-sqlite` builds a SQLite full-text (FTS5) index (`src/schema.ts:127`).
- **What it covers:** the text of past sessions (messages and events), plus details like working directory and creation date. It never reads your source files.
- **Shipped off:** both default profiles set `openAt: never`, and the README says `never` "disables full-text search". Enabling it is a config change to `openAt: startup` or `first-search`.
- **The `@file` path list** from my earlier answer is also lexical in a loose sense. It fuzzy-matches file *names* for the autocomplete dropdown. It's built only when you use `@`, and the model never sees it.
- **Code search:** `grep`/`glob` run ripgrep live on every call and store nothing between calls.

**Graph: nothing at runtime.**
- `packages/typert` has a type-graph generator. It analyzes the **harness's own** TypeScript types at build time to generate its RPC layer, and never looks at your project.
- `scripts/package-graph.ts`, `gen-module-graph.ts` and `gen-doc-graphs.ts` draw dependency diagrams of this repo for its docs. They are developer tooling, not part of the running app.

I confirmed this by searching the package, app and script source for FTS, BM25, TF-IDF, vector databases (FAISS, HNSW, sqlite-vec, LanceDB, Chroma), cosine similarity, graph libraries and call or dependency graphs. Every hit was one of the items above. The agent learns your codebase only by reading and grepping it live during each turn.

Yes, but it's a single agent, not a separate "reasoning agent" and "action agent". The main agent loop in `packages/core/agent-loop` follows the ReAct pattern (reason, act, observe, repeat). Its README sums it up as "call the model, run the tools, repeat."

**How one turn works:**
1. **Reason:** the model thinks before answering. The harness doesn't add a special reasoning step or prompt. It uses the model's built-in thinking (DeepSeek's reasoning output). That thinking is captured as `reasoning` blocks (`packages/llm/llm/src/assembler.ts:112`) and saved to the session log. You can set how hard it thinks with `reasoningEffort` in the config or UI.
2. **Act:** the model calls tools such as `read`, `grep`, `bash` and `edit`. In the default web setup it writes a small program that calls them through a single `run_code` tool. Calls that are safe to run together run in parallel, up to `maxParallelToolCalls: 10`.
3. **Observe:** each tool result is added back to the conversation and the session log.
4. **Repeat:** the loop calls the model again with those results. It stops when the model replies without calling any tools.

**What it doesn't have:**
- No separate planner that hands a plan to a separate executor. Reasoning and actions come from the same model in the same loop.
- No hand-written "Thought / Action / Observation" prompt like the original ReAct paper used. Native tool calling and the model's thinking cover that.
- No reflection or critic agent that reviews answers. The code comment in the `ralph` tool says it plainly: completion "is a worker report, not independent evaluation."

**Optional extras on top of the same loop:**
- **Plan mode:** you switch it on yourself. The same agent plans first, then presents the plan with `exit_plan_mode` for your approval.
- **Subagents and workflows:** the main agent can start child agents. Each child runs the same loop in its own context.
- **Goals:** these keep the loop going across several rounds toward one objective.

== compaction/command-compact/README.md
`dsh-command-compact` adds a `/compact` command to chat UIs: type it and the conversation condenses on demand — the older history is replaced by one summary even before automatic pressure triggers. The command works with any condensation backend and does not consume a model turn; after it finishes you see how many history items were condensed and the estimated tokens saved. While the agent is mid-turn or condensation is already running, it tells you condensation is unavailable. Prompts you send while it runs stay queued and start after it finishes.
== compaction/compaction-basic/README.md
`dsh-compaction-basic` keeps long agent conversations working near the model's context limit. As token pressure builds, it automatically condenses the oldest part of the conversation into a summary and keeps the recent part intact; after a context-overflow error it condenses and retries. You can also condense on demand with `/compact` from `dsh-command-compact`, and mount `dsh-compaction-tool-result-pruner` to trim oversized tool outputs first. Condensation costs one extra model request that reads the selected history and writes the summary; only the summary text is kept. It condenses derived history only — it cannot shrink the system prompt, tools, or session prefix, and one indivisible u
== compaction/compaction-tool-result-pruner/README.md
`dsh-compaction-tool-result-pruner` keeps the context window from filling up with oversized tool output. When compaction is about to run, it trims each over-budget tool result to a bounded head, a short "middle pruned" marker, and a bounded tail, while the full original result stays in the session log for exact replay and inspection. Trimming makes no model call and can clear token pressure on its own, so compaction may skip the summary entirely. It only runs when a compaction trigger qualifies — a below-pressure conversation is never touched. Character budgets are a heuristic; the token meter decides whether pressure was actually relieved.
== compaction/compaction/README.md
`dsh-compaction` lets a long session condense its older history into a single summary message, keep the recent conversation intact, and continue as if the summary had always been there — with a backend such as `dsh-compaction-basic` and the optional `/compact` command. The condensed content stays in the session log, so replaying the session reproduces the exact conversation. Reach for this package when you implement a condensation backend, build something that triggers condensation, or need to recognize condensed messages — it performs no condensation itself. Choose the shipped backend when you just want the feature working out of the box.

No. The model's context has no indexing and no automatic retrieval. There is no RAG step that searches anything and adds relevant pieces to the prompt. Everything in context is either loaded by fixed rules or fetched by the model itself through tools.

**How context is built for each request:**

| Part of context | How it gets there | Indexed or retrieved? |
|---|---|---|
| System prompt and tool descriptions | Fixed text | No |
| `AGENTS.md` / `CLAUDE.md` | Found by walking folders; nested ones are added when the model touches that folder | No, just loading files |
| Conversation history | The session log, in order | No |
| `@file` mentions | You pick a path and the text `@path` goes in your message; the model still has to `read` it | Only the autocomplete path list, which the model never sees |
| `@session` mentions (`session-reference`) | A limited, read-only snapshot of another chat you name. The README says it "needs no SQLite FTS" | Fetched because you named it, not by search |
| Skills | A list of skill names sits in the prompt; the full text loads when the model calls `skill(name)` | Looked up by exact name, not by search |

**When the context gets full:**
- **Compaction** (`compaction-basic`) summarizes the oldest part of the conversation into one message. The originals stay in the session log, but **the model can't get them back**. It only sees the summary.
- **Oversized tool results** are trimmed to a start and end (`compaction-tool-result-pruner`). Alternatively, `spill-policy` saves the full output to a file and gives the model the path, which it can then `read` or `grep`. That's the model retrieving with its tools, not an index.

**The closest thing is only proposed, not built.** `.agents/notes/proposed/feature/2026-07-06-recallable-compaction.md` (status: **proposed**) describes adding exactly this:
- short "index stubs" with keyword lines for each compacted chunk;
- a `history_read` tool so the model can pull summarized history back into context.

Its opening line states the current state plainly: "Compaction is irreversible from the model's current context."

**Summary:** context comes from fixed loading rules, the model's own tool calls, and summarization when space runs out. There's no index to search and no automatic retrieval. The one full-text index (past chat search) is switched off and not wired into context.

It's both: a code pipeline decides when and what to summarize, and **one LLM call** writes the summary. There's no separate summarizer agent and no dedicated summarization model. By default the conversation's own model writes the summary. The code is in `packages/compaction/compaction-basic` and runs in all three web presets (standard, cordis, ptc).

**The pipeline:**

1. **Trigger** (code). Before each request, the token meter measures how much of the context window is used. Summarization starts when:
   - usage passes **80%** of the model's context window (`thresholdRatio 0.8`, `config.ts:20`), or
   - the provider returns a context-overflow error (it summarizes, then retries once), or
   - you type `/compact`.

2. **Trim oversized tool outputs first** (code, no LLM). `compaction-tool-result-pruner` cuts any tool result over 8,192 characters down to its first 4,096 and last 1,024 characters, with a "middle pruned" marker between. If that brings usage back under the limit, the summary step is skipped.

3. **Pick what to summarize** (code, `region.ts`).
   - The most recent **16%** of the context window stays word for word (`retainRatio 0.16`).
   - Everything older is selected for summarizing.
   - The cut points are adjusted so a tool call is never separated from its result.

4. **Summarize** (LLM, `summarizer.ts:121`).
   - **Model:** the conversation's own model by default. `summarizationProvider`/`summarizationModel` can point it at a different one.
   - **Input:** the same system prompt, tool list and selected messages as the last real request. The instruction is added as a final user message. Keeping the start identical lets the provider reuse its cache, so only the instruction is new input.
   - **Format:** the prompt (`summarizer.ts:31-66`) requires exactly these sections: Primary Request and Intent, Key Technical Concepts, Files and Code, Errors and Fixes, Pending Jobs, Current Work, Next Step, Critical Context.
   - **Rules in the prompt:** keep exact paths, commands, error strings and identifiers; quote the user's corrections faithfully; if an earlier summary exists, merge it rather than copy it.
   - **Limit:** 8,192 output tokens.

5. **Check the result** (code). The summary is rejected if it was cut off at the token limit, came back empty, contained images or ended in an error. A failed attempt is retried once (`compactionRetries 1`). Using its token counts, it also checks that the summary is smaller than what it replaces.

6. **Swap it in** (code).
   - The summarized span is replaced by one user message. It starts with a note saying this is an automatic checkpoint to build on without acknowledging, then the summary inside `<compacted-summary>` tags.
   - The original messages stay in the session log, so replaying the session reproduces everything exactly.
   - The model itself can't read the originals back. That's the gap the proposed "recallable compaction" note would fill.

**In short:** the code handles when to summarize, which span, trimming, validation and the swap. The LLM only writes the summary, in one call with a fixed eight-section format. It's a single summarize-everything-older pass, not a chunked or hierarchical pipeline. Chunking plus a `history_read` tool is exactly what the proposed recallable-compaction note describes.

It's plain string cutting, and it only runs as the first step of compaction. It never runs on its own after each tool call. The code is `packages/compaction/compaction-tool-result-pruner/src/index.ts`, called from `compaction-basic/src/index.ts:282-313`. One correction to what I said earlier: the summary can be skipped only for the 80% trigger. After a context-overflow error it always goes on to summarize.

**When it runs**
- **80% trigger:** the context passes 80% of the model's limit. The pruner runs, then usage is measured again. If it's now under 80%, it stops there and no LLM summary is made (`index.ts:309-313`).
- **Overflow error:** the provider rejected the request as too long. The pruner runs, then the summary step runs anyway (`index.ts:284-291`).
- **Otherwise:** tool results are kept whole. The README puts it this way: "a below-pressure conversation is never touched."

**What it does, step by step**

1. **Collect candidates.** It looks at every message the model currently sees and picks out the tool results, such as a `bash` output, a file `read` or a `grep` listing.

2. **Measure each one.** It counts the characters of text in the result.
   - It counts Unicode characters, so an emoji or Chinese character counts as 1.
   - Images count as 0, so they're never cut.
   - Results of **8,192 characters or fewer** are left alone.

3. **Cut out the middle.** For a result over the limit:
   - It keeps the **first 4,096 characters**. Output usually starts with what was run, file headers or the first matches.
   - It keeps the **last 1,024 characters**. Output usually ends with errors, summaries, exit codes or "N tests failed".
   - Everything between is replaced by one marker line: `[... tool result middle pruned ...]`.
   - If the result has several text pieces with images between them, it works across them as one continuous text. Images stay in their original positions, and the marker is inserted once where the cut begins.

   For example, a 50,000-character `npm test` log becomes the first 4,096 characters, the marker, then the last 1,024 characters. That's about 5,160 characters, roughly 90% smaller.

4. **Safety check.** The new version must be smaller than the original and within the limit, or the code throws an error. The cut is by whole characters, so it never splits a multi-byte character into garbage.

5. **Swap it in without deleting anything.** The session log is append-only, so it adds two entries instead of editing the old one:
   - a `compaction/prune` note recording which result was shortened and roughly how many tokens it cost;
   - a new `tool/result` with the shortened content. It keeps the same tool call ID and everything else, and is marked as replacing the original in what the model sees.

   The full original output is still in the log for replay and the UI. The model sees only the shortened version from then on.

6. **Report.** It returns which results were cut and how many characters were removed. Then `compaction-basic` measures token usage again to decide whether an LLM summary is still needed.

**Why do it this way**
- **Cheap and predictable:** no model call and no judgment about what matters, just a fixed rule of keep the start, keep the end, drop the middle.
- **Often enough on its own:** in coding sessions, a few huge outputs (logs, big file reads, long grep results) usually fill most of the context. Trimming them often gets back under 80%, so the slower LLM summary is avoided.
- **Keeps the conversation intact:** unlike summarizing, the order of messages and each tool call and its result stay as they were, only shorter.

**Limits** (from the README)
- It doesn't know what matters. Something important in the middle of an output, like one failing test among thousands of lines, gets dropped.
- The character limits are a rough stand-in for tokens. The token meter makes the real decision about whether it freed enough space.
- The model can't get the removed middle back. The full text is only in

Yes for recent output, mostly no for old output. The tool result is the "observe" step of the loop. Without it the model can't see what `grep` found or why a test failed, and it would guess. Once the model has acted on an output, the full text rarely matters again, and that's exactly the case the pruner targets.

There's a real gap, though. Spill is on by default (`spill-policy`, `maxInlineBytes: 50000` in `packages/bundle/base/cordis.patch.yml:396`), so outputs over about 50 KB are saved to a file the model can reread. Outputs between 8 KB and 50 KB aren't spilled, so when the pruner cuts their middle it's gone for the model, even though it's still in the log.

My recommendation is to have the pruner save the dropped middle through the existing spill store and put the file path in the `[... tool result middle pruned ...]` marker. Trimming would then be recoverable at almost no cost. The tradeoff is more small spill files on disk, and it's a small change within the pruner plugin. Want me to implement it?

The model decides for itself. Nothing makes it open the file, and it never asks you. A file path in the marker is just text, like a note saying "the rest is at /path/x.txt". If the model thinks it needs the missing part, it calls `read` or `grep` on that path itself. Otherwise it ignores the path and carries on.

**When it would read the file**
- The visible start and end aren't enough, for example a test log showing "3 failed" at the end with the failures in the cut middle.
- You ask about something that was in that output.
- It's debugging and needs an exact line, error or value from the middle.

**When it would skip it**
- It already acted on the output, like finishing an edit or a passing build, and has moved on.
- The start and end already show what it needs, such as a command's header and its exit status.

**What can go wrong, and how to limit it**
- **Reading too much:** the model rereads the whole file "just to be safe", which undoes the savings. The marker wording should push it toward targeted access, for example: `[... middle pruned; full text at <path> — grep it or read with offset/limit only if you need the omitted part ...]`.
- **Reading too little:** the model forgets the file exists and guesses. That's better than today, where it can't get the middle back at all.
- **Behavior varies:** how often it reads depends on the model and the wording. Nothing guarantees it, so the useful measure is how often it rereads in real sessions.

It's the same approach the existing spill feature takes for outputs over 50 KB: a preview plus a path, and the model reads the file only when it decides to.

It's a good idea, but I'd add the summary rather than replace the trimmed text with it. Keep the start and end word for word, and put a short LLM summary of the cut middle plus the file path in the marker. The start and end hold the details a summary tends to blur, like the exact command, error strings and exit status. The summary tells the model what was dropped, and the path lets it fetch the exact text when it needs to.

**What you gain**
- The model knows what's in the missing part, so it can decide whether opening the file is worth it instead of guessing.
- Useful facts from the middle, like "3 of 412 tests failed: X, Y, Z", survive even if it never opens the file.

**What it costs**
- **An LLM call.** The pruner is currently free and runs in milliseconds. To keep that cheap, summarize all oversized results in one batched call, ideally with a smaller model, and fall back to plain trimming if the call fails.
- **Less predictable.** Summaries can leave out or misstate details. The path is the safety net, but the model has to notice that it needs to use it.
- **Some overlap with full compaction.** If trimming alone doesn't get usage under 80%, the full conversation summary runs anyway. Summarizing individual outputs pays off only when it avoids that bigger step.

If you want to try it, I'd build it in stages: path-only first (cheap, no model call), then the batched middle summary as an optional setting you can switch on. That way you can compare how often the model rereads with and without the summary. Should I start with the path-only version?

8	const COMPACTION_BUFFER = 20_000
9	
10	export function usable(input: { cfg: ConfigV1.Info; model: Provider.Model; outputTokenMax?: number }) {
11	  const context = input.model.limit.context
12	  if (context === 0) return 0
13	
14	  const reserved =
15	    input.cfg.compaction?.reserved ??
16	    Math.min(COMPACTION_BUFFER, ProviderTransform.maxOutputTokens(input.model, input.outputTokenMax))
17	  return input.model.limit.input
18	    ? Math.max(0, input.model.limit.input - reserved)
19	    : Math.max(0, context - ProviderTransform.maxOutputTokens(input.model, input.outputTokenMax))
20	}
21	
22	export function isOverflow(input: {
23	  cfg: ConfigV1.Info
24	  tokens: SessionV1.Assistant["tokens"]
25	  model: Provider.Model
26	  outputTokenMax?: number
27	}) {
28	  if (input.cfg.compaction?.auto === false) return false
29	  if (input.model.limit.context === 0) return false
30	
31	  const count =
32	    input.tokens.total || input.tokens.input + input.tokens.output + input.tokens.cache.read + input.tokens.cache.write
33	  return count >= usable(input)
34	}

525	export function filterCompacted(msgs: Iterable<WithParts>) {
526	  const result = [] as WithParts[]
527	  const completed = new Set<string>()
528	  let retain: MessageID | undefined
529	  for (const msg of msgs) {
530	    result.push(msg)
531	    if (retain) {
532	      if (msg.info.id === retain) break
533	      continue
534	    }
535	    if (msg.info.role === "user" && completed.has(msg.info.id)) {
536	      const part = msg.parts.find((item): item is CompactionPart => item.type === "compaction")
537	      if (!part) continue
538	      if (!part.tail_start_id) break
539	      retain = part.tail_start_id
540	      if (msg.info.id === retain) break
541	      continue
542	    }
543	    if (msg.info.role === "user" && completed.has(msg.info.id) && msg.parts.some((part) => part.type === "compaction"))
544	      break
545	    if (msg.info.role === "assistant" && msg.info.summary && msg.info.finish && !msg.info.error)
546	      completed.add(msg.info.parentID)
547	  }
548	  result.reverse()
549	  const compactionIndex = result.findLastIndex(
550	    (msg) =>
551	      msg.info.role === "user" &&
552	      msg.parts.some((item): item is CompactionPart => item.type === "compaction" && item.tail_start_id !== undefined),
553	  )
554	  const compaction = result[compactionIndex]
555	  const part = compaction?.parts.find(
556	    (item): item is CompactionPart => item.type === "compaction" && item.tail_start_id !== undefined,
557	  )
558	  const summaryIndex = compaction
559	    ? result.findIndex(
560	        (msg, index) =>
561	          index > compactionIndex &&
562	          msg.info.role === "assistant" &&
563	          msg.info.summary &&
564	          msg.info.parentID === compaction.info.id,
565	      )
566	    : -1
567	  const tailIndex = part?.tail_start_id ? result.findIndex((msg) => msg.info.id === part.tail_start_id) : -1
568	  if (tailIndex >= 0 && tailIndex < compactionIndex && summaryIndex > compactionIndex) {
569	    return [
570	      ...result.slice(compactionIndex, summaryIndex + 1),
571	      ...result.slice(tailIndex, compactionIndex),
572	      ...result.slice(summaryIndex + 1),
573	    ]
574	  }
575	  return result
576	}

I read opencode's source directly: `github.com/sst/opencode` at commit `b471c2b` (2026-09-26). Everything below comes from that code, with file and line references. Like ours, it uses **one LLM call** for the summary with code around it, plus an optional pruner that makes no LLM call.

The app's main loop (`packages/opencode/src/session/prompt.ts`) uses `packages/opencode/src/session/compaction.ts`. There's also a simpler second version in `packages/core/src/session/compaction.ts`, but the app's loop only borrows its prompt template (`buildPrompt`). I cover that second version briefly at the end.

### 1. When it runs
- **Auto trigger:** after each model step, `isOverflow` (`overflow.ts:22-34`) checks whether the tokens used, cache included, have reached the "usable" limit.
- **Usable limit:** the model's input limit minus a reserve of min(20,000, max output tokens). If the model has no separate input limit, it's the context window minus max output. So it triggers close to full, not at a percentage like our 80%.
- **Provider error:** it also runs when the provider rejects a request as too long (`processor.ts:493`), and when you run `/compact` yourself.
- **Off switch:** `compaction.auto: false` in the config disables the automatic trigger.

### 2. Pruning old tool outputs (`compaction.ts:273-317`)
- **Off by default.** The config schema says: `prune` — "Enable pruning of old tool outputs (default: false)".
- **When:** it runs in the background *after* the agent loop finishes (`prompt.ts:1338`), not as a first step before summarizing.
- **How it picks outputs:**
  - It walks backwards through history, skipping the last 2 user turns.
  - The most recent **40,000 tokens** of tool output are protected (`PRUNE_PROTECT`).
  - Output from the `skill` tool is never pruned.
  - It stops at a previous summary or at outputs already pruned.
  - It acts only if at least **20,000 tokens** can be freed (`PRUNE_MINIMUM`).
- **What it does:** each selected output is replaced **entirely** by `[Old tool result content cleared]` (`message-v2.ts:297-298`). It keeps no start or end and gives no file path. The original stays in storage, flagged as cleared.

### 3. Summarizing
1. **Keep a recent tail word for word.**
   - The budget is `preserve_recent_tokens`, by default 25% of the usable limit, clamped between **2,000 and 15,000** tokens (`compaction.ts:115-120`).
   - It walks backwards over whole user turns and can split a turn if needed. `tail_turns` can also cap how many turns are kept.
2. **Turn the older part into a plain-text transcript** (`serialize`, `compaction.ts:54-85`).
   - Each item gets a label: `[User]:`, `[Assistant]:`, `[Assistant reasoning]:`, `[Assistant tool call]: name({json})` and `[Tool result]: ...`.
   - **Each tool result is cut to its first 2,000 characters** plus `[truncated]`. Pruned results appear as `[Old tool result content cleared]`.
   - Attachments become placeholders like `[Attached image/png: x.png]`.
3. **Merge any earlier summary.** The previous summary is passed in `<prior-summary>` tags with merge rules: carry forward goals and decisions, newer facts win, move finished work from "Active" to "Completed". The old summary messages are left out of the new transcript.
4. **Plugin hooks:** `experimental.session.compacting` lets plugins add context or replace the prompt entirely (`compaction.ts:373`).
5. **The LLM call:**

Overall ours is stronger, mainly because the summarizer sees more of the conversation and costs less. opencode does two things better: its pruning spares recent outputs, and its rules for merging an earlier summary are more explicit. This is my judgment from reading both codebases. Neither project publishes benchmarks comparing them.

**Where ours is better**
- **Summary quality:** our summarizer sees the real conversation, including tool outputs up to 8k characters (longer ones pruned to their first 4k and last 1k). opencode cuts every tool result to its first 2,000 characters before summarizing, so errors near the end of a long output never reach its summarizer.
- **Cost and speed:** we replay the exact last request, so the provider reuses its cache and only the instruction is new input. opencode rewrites history as a new text transcript, so the whole thing is billed as fresh input.
- **Verbatim tail on large models:** we keep 16% of the context window word for word, which grows with the model. opencode caps it at 15,000 tokens even on a 1M-token model.
- **Safety margin:** we trigger at 80%. opencode waits until it's nearly full, which means a lot of overflow-error recoveries.

**Where opencode is better**
- **Which outputs get pruned:** it protects the last 2 turns and the most recent 40,000 tokens of tool output, and prunes only older ones. Ours cuts *every* oversized tool result, including the one the model is working with right now (`pruneSession` loops over all tool results with no recency check).
- **Merging an earlier summary:** its rules are explicit (newer facts win, move finished work from Active to Completed, anything not carried forward is lost). Ours has a single line about this.
- **A clean summarizer:** a tool-less agent can't wander off. Ours sends the tool list for cache reuse and relies on the instruction plus a text-only filter.

**Where both fall short:** neither lets the model get cut or summarized content back.

**What I'd do:** keep our design and add three things:
1. **Recency protection in our pruner:** skip the last N turns or tokens of tool output, like opencode.
2. **A spill path in the prune marker:** save the cut middle and point to it, as discussed earlier.
3. **Explicit merge rules for an earlier summary** in our compaction instruction.

All three are small and stay inside the compaction plugins. Want me to start with #1? It fixes the biggest weakness.

Here's the side-by-side comparison, built from the code of both projects: our repo, and opencode at commit `b471c2b`.

### Trigger

| | Elemental Harness (`compaction-basic`) | opencode (`session/compaction.ts`) |
|---|---|---|
| Automatic trigger | Token usage ≥ **80%** of context window (`thresholdRatio 0.8`) | Tokens used ≥ **usable limit** = input limit − min(20k, max output), i.e. nearly full |
| Provider overflow error | Prunes, summarizes, retries (up to `maxOverflowRetries: 1`) | Compacts, then re-sends the interrupted user message; media replaced by placeholders |
| Manual | `/compact` | `/compact` |
| Turn off | `auto: false` | `compaction.auto: false` |
| Per-model settings | Yes (`modelPolicies`) | No; one global config |

### Stage 1: pruning tool outputs (no LLM)

| | Elemental Harness (`compaction-tool-result-pruner`) | opencode (`prune`) |
|---|---|---|
| Default | **On** in the web presets | **Off** (`prune: false`) |
| When it runs | Only when compaction triggers, before summarizing | After every completed agent loop, in the background, whether or not the context is full |
| Which outputs | **Every** tool result over 8,192 characters, including the latest | Only **older** outputs: skips the last 2 turns, protects the newest 40k tokens of output, never prunes `skill` |
| Minimum gain | None; any oversized result is cut | Acts only if ≥ **20k tokens** can be freed |
| What replaces it | First **4,096** chars + `[... tool result middle pruned ...]` + last **1,024** chars | The whole output becomes `[Old tool result content cleared]` |
| Original kept? | Yes, in the append-only log | Yes, in storage, flagged as cleared |
| Can the model get it back? | No | No |
| Can it avoid the LLM summary? | Yes: if usage drops below 80% after pruning, the summary is skipped (pressure trigger only) | No; the two are separate |

### Stage 2: choosing what to summarize

| | Elemental Harness | opencode |
|---|---|---|
| Kept word for word | Newest **16% of the context window** (`retainRatio 0.16`), or a fixed `retainTokens` | Newest **2k–15k tokens**: 25% of the usable limit, clamped |
| Cut point | Moved so a tool call is never separated from its result | Walks back over whole user turns, can split a turn; `tail_turns` can cap it |
| Summarized | Everything older than the kept part | Everything older than the kept part, minus earlier summary messages |

### Stage 3: the summary LLM call

| | Elemental Harness | opencode |
|---|---|---|
| Who summarizes | The conversation's own model by default; can be set to another (`summarizationProvider`/`Model`) | A hidden **"compaction" agent** with all tools denied; its own model if set, otherwise the conversation's |
| Format of the input | **Exact replay** of the last request: same system prompt, same tools, same messages | A **new plain-text transcript** (`[User]:`, `[Assistant]:`, `[Assistant reasoning]:`, `[Tool result]:` …) |
| Tool outputs in the input | As they are (already pruned to first 4k and last 1k if large) | Each **cut to its first 2,000 characters** + `[truncated]` |
| System prompt | The conversation's own | "You are a context summarization agent… Do not continue the conversation…" |
| Tools available | Tool list sent (for cache reuse); told not to call any | None |
| Provider cache reuse | **Yes**; only the final instruction is new input | **No**; the whole transcript is fresh input |
| Summary sections | Primary Request and Intent · Key Technical Concepts · Files and Code · Errors and Fixes · Pending Jobs · Current Work · Next Step · Critical Context | Objective · Important Details · Work State (Completed / Active / Blocked) · Next Move · Relevant Files |
| Key rules | Keep exact paths, commands, errors and IDs; quote user corrections faithfully; don't mention compaction | Keep exact paths, commands, errors, URLs and IDs; terse bullets; reply in the conversation's language; don't mention compaction |

Yes. Here's what I'd improve, most important first:

1. **Stop the pruner cutting recent tool output.** This is the one real bug-like weakness. `pruneSession` (`compaction-tool-result-pruner/src/index.ts:136-146`) cuts every tool result over 8k characters, including the one the model is reading right now. The fix is to protect the last N turns or tokens of tool output, as opencode does. It's a small change in one plugin.

2. **Put a file path in the prune marker.** Save the cut middle through the existing spill store and write its path into `[... tool result middle pruned ...]`. Trimming then becomes recoverable, and the model reads the file only when it needs to. It's cheap and needs no LLM call.

3. **Spell out how to merge an earlier summary.** Replace the single line in `COMPACTION_INSTRUCTION` (`compaction-basic/src/summarizer.ts:65`) with explicit rules:
   - newer facts win;
   - move finished work out of the in-progress sections;
   - keep user directives even if recent turns don't mention them;
   - anything not carried forward is lost.

   This matters most in long sessions that get compacted several times. It's a prompt-only change.

4. **Let the model recall summarized history.** This is the bigger feature from the proposed recallable-compaction note (`.agents/notes/proposed/feature/2026-07-06-recallable-compaction.md`): short index entries per summarized chunk plus a `history_read` tool. Neither harness has this today. It's the largest item, so I'd do it last.

**Worth measuring, not changing blindly:**
- **80% trigger and 16% kept tail:** reasonable defaults, but I'd first check real sessions to see how often compaction fires and whether the model then rereads files it had already seen.
- **Tool list in the summary call:** we send the tool list only to reuse the provider's cache. I'd check the logs for summary calls where the model tried to call a tool anyway before changing anything.

Items 1–3 are small, stay inside the compaction plugins, and each needs a test, a snapshot update and an Agent Note under this repo's rules. Want me to start with #1?

> ## Documentation Index

# Manage costs effectively

> Track token usage, set team spend limits, and reduce Claude Code costs with context management, model selection, extended thinking settings, and preprocessing hooks.

Claude Code charges by API token consumption. For subscription plan pricing (Pro, Max, Team, Enterprise), see [claude.com/pricing](https://claude.com/pricing). Per-developer costs vary widely based on model selection, codebase size, and usage patterns such as running multiple instances or automation.

Across enterprise deployments, the average cost is around \$13 per developer per active day and \$150-250 per developer per month, with costs remaining below \$30 per active day for 90% of users. To estimate spend for your own team, start with a small pilot group and use the tracking tools below to establish a baseline before wider rollout.

This page covers how to [track your costs](#track-your-costs), [manage costs for your organization](#manage-costs-for-your-organization), and [reduce token usage](#reduce-token-usage).

## Track your costs

### Using the `/usage` command

<Note>
  The Session block in `/usage` shows API token usage and is intended for API users. Claude Max and Pro subscribers have usage included in their subscription, so the session cost figure isn't relevant for billing purposes. Subscribers see plan usage bars, activity stats, and a usage breakdown on the same screen.
</Note>

The Session block at the top of `/usage` shows detailed token usage statistics for your current session. Claude Code computes the dollar figure locally from token counts at list price, unless a [`modelPricing`](/docs/en/settings-reference#modelpricing) table is in effect. An administrator sets one in your organization's managed settings so the figure uses your contracted rates, and while a table is in effect the `Total cost` line carries the note `at your organization's configured rates`. The figure is an estimate, so for authoritative billing see the Usage page in the [Claude Console](https://platform.claude.com/usage).

I read this from the Claude Code binary installed on your machine (`~/.local/bin/claude.exe`, **v2.1.281**) and from Anthropic's cost docs (code.claude.com/docs/en/costs). The code is minified, so function names are meaningless, but the numbers, prompts and messages below are literal from the binary.

Several behaviors are switched by remote feature flags (named like `tengu_*`). The binary shows each flag's default, but not whether it's turned on for your account. I say where that matters.

Claude Code manages context in **four layers**.

### 1. Big tool outputs are saved to disk immediately

This happens as each tool returns, not at compaction time.
- **Threshold:** if a tool result is over that tool's size limit (400,000 characters when a tool sets none), the full output goes to a file named after the tool call ID in the session folder.
- **What the model gets instead:**
  ```
  <persisted-output>
  Output too large (X). Full output saved to: <path>
  Preview (first 2KB):
  ...
  </persisted-output>
  ```
  The preview is cut at a line break when possible.
- **If saving fails:** it sends `<truncated-output>` with the first part and the advice "If the tool can page or filter its results, call it again for the part you need."
- **Empty results** become `(<tool> completed with no output)`.
- **Images and documents** are never saved this way.

### 2. Old tool results are cleared, recent ones kept ("microcompact")
- **Scope:** only certain tools' results can be cleared, including Read (the code tracks which file paths were cleared).
- **What's kept:** the **5 most recent** results are always kept.
- **When it acts:** older results are cleared only if that frees at least **20,000 tokens**. Images count as 2,000 tokens each.
- **What replaces a cleared result:** a `<persisted-output>` pointer to its saved file if saving works, otherwise `[Old tool result content cleared]`. **The model can reread a cleared result from disk**, which neither our harness nor opencode allows.
- **Trigger:** when the API rejects a request with a "context hint" (HTTP 422/424), and on some retry paths. This path is behind flag `tengu_hazel_osprey`, **default off**, with a 75,000-token floor.
- **The docs confirm it exists:** they count "clearing old tool results from context" as an expected cache rebuild.

### 3. Auto-compaction threshold
- **Formula:**
  - *Effective window* = auto-compact window − min(model's max output tokens, 20,000)
  - **Compacts at** effective window − **13,000** tokens.
  - A warning appears 20,000 tokens before that.
  - Requests are blocked at the full limit − 3,000.
- **Example:** a 200k window with a 20k output reserve gives an effective 180k, so it compacts at **167k (~83%)**.
- **Auto-compact window:**
  - defaults to the model's context window;
  - some models billed above 200k are capped at **200,000**;
  - `claude-sonnet-5` defaults to **1,000,000** (500,000 on some surfaces);
  - you can override it with `/autocompact`, `CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW` or `CLAUDE_AUTOCOMPACT_PCT_OVERRIDE`;
  - `DISABLE_AUTO_COMPACT` and `DISABLE_COMPACT` switch compaction off.
- **Earlier start:** a separate "precompute" threshold at 80% of the effective window (flag-controlled fraction, default 0.2). Its name suggests it starts preparing the summary early.
- **Thrashing guard:** if the context refills within 3 turns of a compaction, 3 times in a row, it stops with: *"Autocompact is thrashing… A file being read or a tool output is likely too large for the context window…"*

### 4. The summary (one LLM call)

**The prompt** (verbatim headings):
- It opens with *"Your task is to create a detailed summary of the conversation so far…"*
- The model first writes an **`<analysis>`** block as scratch reasoning, then a **`<summary>`**. The code strips the analysis with a regex and keeps only the summary.
- Nine sections: **Primary Request and Intent · Key Technical Concepts · Files and Code Sections** (with full code snippets) **· Errors and fixe

Here's the strategy I'd build. It keeps our strengths (the cache-reusing summary and the append-only log) and adds what Claude Code does better. The main idea: keep recent content exact, make anything removed recoverable, and use the LLM summary only as the last resort.

### The plan, in five layers

**1. When a tool returns: save big outputs to disk early**
- Today only outputs over 50 KB are saved to a file (`spill-policy`, `maxInlineBytes: 50000`). Claude Code saves anything over its limit to a file and gives the model a 2 KB preview plus the path.
- I'd lower our threshold so more large outputs go to disk up front and never bloat the context. It's a one-line setting change; the right number should come from real sessions.

**2. When compaction triggers: a smarter pruner (no LLM)**
- **Protect recent output:** never cut the last few tool results or the current turn. Claude Code keeps the last 5; opencode protects the newest 40k tokens. This fixes our biggest weakness.
- **Only prune when it's worth it:** skip pruning unless it frees a meaningful amount, around 20k tokens. Both other harnesses use this bar, because each prune breaks the provider cache.
- **Make cuts recoverable:** save the cut part through the spill store and put the path in the marker. The first and last characters stay visible, so the model can decide whether it needs the rest.

**3. The summary (one LLM call): better prompt, same design**
- **Keep** the exact-replay design, which Claude Code and opencode don't have and which keeps our summary call cheap.
- **Add from Claude Code:**
  - an "All user messages" section, listed word for word;
  - security constraints the user gave, kept word for word;
  - the next step with a verbatim quote of where the work left off.
- **Add from opencode:** explicit rules for merging an earlier summary (newer facts win, finished work moves out of "in progress", anything not carried forward is lost).

**4. After compaction: a way back to the originals**
- **Session log path:** the checkpoint message should include the path to the session's JSONL log and say how to search it with `grep` or `read`. Claude Code does exactly this with its transcript path.
- **Re-attach recently read files:** add a few recently read files back, within a token budget. Claude Code uses 5 files, 5k tokens each, 50k total. `fs-observation-policy` already tracks which files the model has read, so we can build on it.
- Under our "model-visible ⟺ logged" rule, both have to be written as session events. That fits our event-log design.

**5. Guardrails**
- **Stop thrashing:** if the context refills within a few turns of compaction several times in a row, stop and tell the user a file or output is too big, as Claude Code does. Today we'd keep compacting forever.

**Later:** the recallable-compaction proposal (short index entries plus a `history_read` tool). Layer 4 gets most of its benefit far more cheaply, so this can wait.

### Suggested order

| Phase | What | Size | Why first |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Pruner: protect recent output, minimum gain, path in the marker | Small, one plugin | Fixes the biggest weakness; no LLM cost |
| 2 | Summary prompt: user messages, security constraints, verbatim next step, merge rules | Small, prompt only | Better summaries at no extra cost |
| 3 | After compaction: log path + re-attached files | Medium | Makes summaries recoverable |
| 4 | Thrashing guard | Small | Safety |
| 5 | Lower the spill threshold | One setting | Tune it with data from phases 1–3 |

Each phase needs a test, a snapshot update and an Agent Note under this repo's rules. I'd start with Phase 1. Want me to go ahead?

1	/** Configuration resolution for deterministic tool-result pruning. */
2	
3	import { deepFreeze } from '@deepseek-ai/dsh-util-values'
4	import type { ResolvedConfig, ToolResultPruneConfig } from './types.ts'
5	
6	/** Fixed marker substituted for every removed middle span. */
7	export const PRUNE_MARKER = '\n\n[... tool result middle pruned ...]\n\n'
8	
9	/** Low-friction defaults for coding-agent tool output. */
10	export const DEFAULTS: ResolvedConfig = deepFreeze({
11	  thresholdChars: 8192,
12	  headChars: 4096,
13	  tailChars: 1024,
14	})
15	
16	const CONFIG_KEYS: ReadonlySet<string> = new Set([
17	  'thresholdChars',
18	  'headChars',
19	  'tailChars',
20	])
21	
22	/**
23	 * Count Unicode code points without splitting surrogate pairs.
24	 * @param text - text to measure.
25	 * @returns the Unicode code-point count.
26	 */
27	export function codePointLength(text: string): number {
28	  return Array.from(text).length
29	}
30	
31	/**
32	 * Resolve and validate pruning budgets.
33	 * @param config - raw plugin configuration.
34	 * @returns a detached deeply immutable configuration.
35	 */
36	export function resolveConfig(config: ToolResultPruneConfig = {}): ResolvedConfig {
37	  for (const key of Object.keys(config)) {
38	    if (!CONFIG_KEYS.has(key)) {
39	      throw new Error(
40	        `ToolResultPruneConfig: unknown key "${key}" `
41	        + '(allowed: thresholdChars, headChars, tailChars)',
42	      )
43	    }
44	  }
45	
46	  const resolved: ResolvedConfig = {
47	    thresholdChars: config.thresholdChars ?? DEFAULTS.thresholdChars,
48	    headChars: config.headChars ?? DEFAULTS.headChars,
49	    tailChars: config.tailChars ?? DEFAULTS.tailChars,
50	  }
51	  assertPositiveInteger('thresholdChars', resolved.thresholdChars)
52	  assertNonNegativeInteger('headChars', resolved.headChars)
53	  assertNonNegativeInteger('tailChars', resolved.tailChars)
54	
55	  const emittedChars = resolved.headChars
56	    + codePointLength(PRUNE_MARKER)
57	    + resolved.tailChars
58	  if (emittedChars > resolved.thresholdChars) {
59	    throw new Error(
60	      `ToolResultPruneConfig: headChars + marker + tailChars (${emittedChars}) `
61	      + `must be at most thresholdChars (${resolved.thresholdChars})`,
62	    )
63	  }
64	  return deepFreeze(structuredClone(resolved))
65	}
66	
67	function assertPositiveInteger(name: string, value: number): void {
68	  if (!Number.isInteger(value) || value <= 0) {
69	    throw new Error(`ToolResultPruneConfig: ${name} (${value}) must be a positive integer`)
70	  }
71	}
72	
73	function assertNonNegativeInteger(name: string, value: number): void {
74	  if (!Number.isInteger(value) || value < 0) {
75	    throw new Error(`ToolResultPruneConfig: ${name} (${value}) must be a non-negative integer`)
76	  }
77	}
78

1	import type { ToolCallId } from '@deepseek-ai/dsh-llm'
2	
3	/** Character-budget policy for deterministic tool-result pruning. */
4	export interface ToolResultPruneConfig {
5	  /** Prune when total text exceeds this many Unicode code points. Defaults to `8192`. */
6	  thresholdChars?: number
7	  /** Maximum leading Unicode code points retained. Defaults to `4096`. */
8	  headChars?: number
9	  /** Maximum trailing Unicode code points retained. Defaults to `1024`. */
10	  tailChars?: number
11	}
12	
13	/** Validated, detached, deeply immutable pruning configuration. */
14	export interface ResolvedConfig {
15	  readonly thresholdChars: number
16	  readonly headChars: number
17	  readonly tailChars: number
18	}
19	
20	/** Cited source event and size accounting for one landed surface replacement. */
21	export interface PrunedEntry {
22	  /** Full-fidelity tool-result event shadowed by the replacement. */
23	  readonly originalSeq: number
24	  /** Newly appended pruned tool-result event. */
25	  readonly replacementSeq: number
26	  /** Tool call shared by the original and replacement. */
27	  readonly callId: ToolCallId
28	  /** Original text size in Unicode code points. */
29	  readonly charsBefore: number
30	  /** Replacement text size in Unicode code points. */
31	  readonly charsAfter: number
32	}
33	
34	/** Aggregate outcome of one stable-surface pruning pass. */
35	export interface PruneResult {
36	  /** Replacements in the snapshotted surface order. */
37	  readonly pruned: readonly PrunedEntry[]
38	  /** Total Unicode code points removed across replacements. */
39	  readonly charsRemoved: number
40	}

1	/**
2	 * Vocabulary for the spill storage Service Definition. Types only — the abstract service
3	 * lives in `./index.ts`, implementations in sibling packages
4	 * (`@deepseek-ai/dsh-spill-local` first).
5	 *
6	 * @module @deepseek-ai/dsh-spill/types
7	 */
8	
9	import type { Branded } from '@deepseek-ai/dsh-brand'
10	import type { ToolCallId } from '@deepseek-ai/dsh-llm'
11	import type { SessionId } from '@deepseek-ai/dsh-session'
12	
13	/**
14	 * Opaque model-facing handle for one spilled artifact. A local backend may use a
15	 * filesystem path; a remote or database backend may use a URI or key. Consumers
16	 * render it with {@link SpillRef.retrievalHint}, but do not parse it.
17	 */
18	export type SpillLocator = Branded<'SpillLocator'>
19	
20	/**
21	 * Brand a string as a {@link SpillLocator}.
22	 *
23	 * @param locator The backend-produced locator string to brand.
24	 * @returns The branded spill locator.
25	 */
26	export function SpillLocator(locator: string): SpillLocator {
27	  return locator as SpillLocator
28	}
29	
30	/**
31	 * Save-time storage namespace for a spilled artifact. The session id lets a
32	 * backend group storage under the producing session, but the returned
33	 * {@link SpillLocator} is the model-facing handle. Forked sessions inherit
34	 * locators already present in the seeded log; those artifacts are not copied or
35	 * re-owned, and spills produced after the fork use the child session id.
36	 */
37	export interface SpillOwner {
38	  sessionId: SessionId
39	}
40	
41	/**
42	 * Tool and call that produced one spilled artifact — recorded by the backend for a readable
43	 * filename and inspection. Not interpreted for access control; purely
44	 * descriptive.
45	 */
46	export interface SpillSource {
47	  /** The tool whose result was spilled (e.g. `web_fetch`). */
48	  toolName: string
49	  /** The model-issued call id the result belongs to. */
50	  callId: ToolCallId
51	  /** A short human label for the artifact (e.g. `result`). */
52	  label: string
53	}
54	
55	/** One request to persist text to a spill artifact. */
56	export interface SaveTextSpill {
57	  owner: SpillOwner
58	  source: SpillSource
59	  /**
60	   * A caller-suggested base name (e.g. `web_fetch.txt`). The backend sanitizes
61	   * it to a single safe path segment before use — it is a hint, never a path.
62	   */
63	  suggestedName: string
64	  /** The full text to persist (UTF-8). */
65	  content: string
66	}
67	
68	/** A saved spill artifact: its locator, byte length, and backend-specific retrieval guidance. */
69	export interface SpillRef {
70	  locator: SpillLocator
71	  bytes: number
72	  retrievalHint: string
73	}

5	- **Plugin exports:** service packages default-export their service class; function plugins named-export `name` / `inject` / `Config` / `apply` and have no default export. Mixing the forms makes the Loader discard the function plugin's namespace ([postmortem](../docs/postmortem/0001-acp-default-export-drops-inject.md)).
6	- **Optional services use `ctx.get(name)`.** Reserve `ctx.<name>` for declared injections; the property proxy is topology-sensitive, while strict `ctx.get` reads the global service store ([postmortem](../docs/postmortem/0001-acp-default-export-drops-inject.md)).
7	- **Product-visible plugins require a non-unit REAL-composition test.** Hand-built `ctx.plugin(...)` suites are insufficient. Boot test-only `cordis.yml` through the Loader and app/process; mock only external services or nondeterministic inputs and assert model-visible, durable, or user-visible output. Keep opt-ins out of shipped defaults. [Policy](../docs/testing.md).
8	- **Initiator-owned private chains derive, then capture.** Under `ctx.agents.withInitiator()`, recover the Agent at each orchestration entry, derive `agent.session`, and let operation-local helpers close over it. Keep `Agent` and `Session` explicit at lifecycle, session-log, service, authority, worker/process, persistence, and wire interfaces; do not widen a leaf helper from `Session` to `Context` merely to hide a parameter ([rationale](../.agents/notes/implemented/architecture/2026-07-15-agent-initiator-scope.md)).
9	- **Represent one asynchronous operation with one lifecycle controller or transaction.** Separate readiness, cancellation, disposal, reservation, or sentinel state requires an independent owner or settlement point; otherwise fold it while preserving rollback, callback containment, and quiescence.
10	- **Design Service Definitions for all current Consumers.** Keep tool-schema, Loader, UI, transport, and provider-specific behavior in the Consumer or provider; do not let one Consumer dictate the service contract ([capability-seam rationale](../.agents/notes/implemented/architecture/2026-06-13-capability-seams.md)). Inverse smell: a public service method with one internal caller — pass a private capability closure instead (`RunCodeBridgeOptions`).
11	- **Require a current owner and need.** Tie each abstraction, state machine, option, defensive copy, and compatibility path to a current contract or production consumer, and keep behavior in its owning plugin or service.
12	- **Require evidence for public choices.** Configurability does not justify an unsupported default, public operation set, format, or imported external concept. Use current-consumer evidence or relevant prior art; otherwise require an explicit value or defer the choice.

4	 * locator plus retrieval guidance — without saying HOW. Implementations

6	 * `@deepseek-ai/dsh-spill-local` (host filesystem) is the first.

8	 * The Service Definition is deliberately minimal: `saveText` and nothing else. It owns NO
9	 * retention policy (that is `@deepseek-ai/dsh-output-retention`), NO tool-result
10	 * replacement (that is `@deepseek-ai/dsh-spill-policy`), and NO retrieval or
11	 * search API. The backend supplies the locator and retrieval hint appropriate

29	/**
30	 * Abstract spill storage service. Subclass, implement {@link saveText}, and load
31	 * the subclass as a plugin — it registers as `ctx.spillStore` (one
32	 * implementation per context; loading a second throws, cordis' standard
33	 * duplicate-service behavior).
34	 *
35	 * Semantics every implementation must honor:
36	 * - {@link saveText} persists the FULL `content` verbatim and returns an opaque
37	 *   locator, exact byte length, and model-facing retrieval guidance.
38	 * - Storage is scoped by the request's {@link SaveTextSpill.owner} session; the
39	 *   backend chooses a private (not world-readable) location and a collision-free
40	 *   name derived from — never equal to — the caller's `suggestedName`.
41	 * - `saveText` REJECTS on a real storage failure (permissions, ENOSPC, backend
42	 *   unavailable); the caller decides how to degrade (the spill policy treats a
43	 *   rejection as best-effort and keeps the inline result).
44	 */

47	    super(ctx, 'spillStore')

49

52	   * @param input - the owner, caller-supplied source fields, suggested name, and full text to save.
53	   * @returns the saved artifact's {@link SpillRef}; rejects on a storage failure.
54	   */

1	/**
2	 * The spill-policy PLUGIN: a `tools/post-execute` result transformer that keeps
3	 * oversized plain-text tool results out of the model's context. When a final
4	 * result's UTF-8 size exceeds `maxInlineBytes`, it saves the FULL text to a
5	 * session-scoped spill artifact (`ctx.spillStore`) and replaces the
6	 * model-facing result with a bounded head/tail preview plus the backend's
7	 * locator and retrieval guidance.
8	 *
9	 * It registers NO service and owns NO storage or preview mechanics: preview is
10	 * `@deepseek-ai/dsh-output-retention` (`TextRetainer`), storage is `ctx.spillStore`.
11	 * The policy only decides WHEN to spill and composes the notice.
12	 *
13	 * A second arm applies the SAME cap to the durable log: the
14	 * `tools/ptc-dispatch-log` waterfall bounds the `tool/code-dispatch` event's
15	 * copy of an oversized `run_code` sub-call result (the program's value is
16	 * untouched; UIs and replay read the full text through the spill artifact).
17	 *
18	 * ## Deliberately narrow
19	 *
20	 * - Omitted `maxInlineBytes` ⇒ the plugin registers nothing (a true no-op).
21	 * - Plain-text results only: a result carrying any non-text block is left
22	 *   untouched (the policy knows only the final formatted text, not tool
23	 *   internals).
24	 * - Nested composite calls skip the MODEL-facing arm; their durable log copy
25	 *   is bounded by the dispatch-log arm instead.
26	 * - Accepted value replacements pass through for registry revalidation and
27	 *   rendering; this presentation policy cannot also replace content in the
28	 *   same mutually exclusive decision.
29	 * - `read` is skipped by the model-facing arm to avoid a
30	 *   `read → spill → read again` loop; the dispatch-log arm bounds `read`
31	 *   sub-calls too (a log copy is not model context, and `read` is precisely
32	 *   the tool that produces huge logs).
33	 * - Best-effort: no session owner, no `ctx.spillStore` backend, or a save
34	 *   failure ⇒ log and return the original result. A spill failure must NEVER
35	 *   turn a successful tool call into an `isError` or hide the inline result.
36	 *
37	 * It COMPOSES with other post-execute listeners: its prepended listener
38	 * delegates via `next()` and bounds the resulting content projection, so
39	 * tool-owned asynchronous projection runs before generic bounding, a hook that
40	 * replaced content still has its replacement bounded, and value replacements
41	 * and `block` decisions pass through unchanged.
42	 *
43	 * @module @deepseek-ai/dsh-spill-policy
44	 */

1	---
2	description: "Tool-output trimming for deployments composing compaction: choosing size limits or debugging why oversized tool results get shortened."

5	
6	# @deepseek-ai/dsh-compaction-tool-result-pruner
7	
8	## Summary
9	
10	`dsh-compaction-tool-result-pruner` keeps the context window from filling up with oversized tool output. When compaction is about to run, it trims each over-budget tool result to a bounded head, a short "middle pruned" marker, and a bounded tail, while the full original result stays in the session log for exact replay and inspection. Trimming makes no model call and can clear token pressure on its own, so compaction may skip the summary entirely. It only runs when a compaction trigger qualifies — a below-pressure conversation is never touched. Character budgets are a heuristic; the token meter decides whether pressure was actually relieved.
11	
12	## Table of Contents
13	
14	- [Use this package](#use-this-package)
15	- [Understand the implementation](#understand-the-implementation)
16	- [Further Exploration](#further-exploration)
17	- [Model Experience](#model-experience)
18	- [Known Limitations and Deferred Work](#known-limitations-and-deferred-work)
19	- [Dev Note](#dev-note)
20	
21	-----
22	
23	<a id="use-this-package"></a>
24	## Use this package
25	
26	Mount this package next to `dsh-compaction-basic` when tool output regularly dominates the conversation window. Trimming changes what the model sees — shorter results — and gives compaction less history to condense.
27	
28	### Smallest working composition
29	
30	Mount token measurement, this package, and the backend in this order:
31	
32	```yaml
33	- name: '@deepseek-ai/dsh-token-meter'
34	- name: '@deepseek-ai/dsh-compaction-tool-result-pruner'
35	- name: '@deepseek-ai/dsh-compaction-basic'
36	```
37	
38	With these rows, oversized tool results are trimmed automatically as part of condensation. You can verify success by checking that future requests show the trimmed results; the full originals remain in the session log.
39	
40	### What gets trimmed
41	
42	Every tool result whose text exceeds the threshold is replaced by a trimmed version: the configured head, a short "middle pruned" marker, and the configured tail. Rich content such as images and structured blocks keeps its order. The replacement keeps the tool call, step, errors, and metadata — only the text content changes. If a replacement cannot be recorded, the run fails and the trims already applied stay in place.
43	
44	### Setting the size limits
45

```
# Agent Notes

One kind of design doc lives here. An **Agent Note** records a decision or proposal that affects this codebase — the *why* and *what we gave up*, the parts code and docs can't carry. This file defines where Agent Notes live, when to write one, and [the in-file format](#the-file-format).

## Layout and naming

Every Agent Note has two axes, both encoded in its **path** — `{lifecycle}/{class}/yyyy-mm-dd-topic-title.md`:

- **Lifecycle** (the top-level folder) is the Agent Note's status, and an Agent Note moves between folders as that status changes:
  - **`proposed/`** — proposals reviewed before implementation; not yet built (or only partly).
  - **`implemented/`** — the decision shipped. The file records what was decided and what was rejected, and is **kept current with what actually shipped**: when the code later moves a file, renames a package, or changes a key/default, the Agent Note is updated in the same change to match (facts only — paths, names, structure — not the decision itself). See [implemented/AGENTS.md](implemented/AGENTS.md).
  - **`rejected/`** — the proposal was considered and declined. Keep it only while its rationale prevents a tempting, meaningful mistake; otherwise delete the complete triplet.
- **Class** (the nested folder) is the *kind* of decision — see [Classification](#classification) below.

The date in the filename is when the topic was **first proposed** (per git history). Cross-references between Agent Notes use relative markdown links (`topic`) — never bare prose or numbers — so they are mechanically checkable and survive moves between folders.

The active lifecycle tree is the working inventory: browse its lifecycle/class folders or search the repository. Do not add a centralized `INDEX.md`; the [no-index Agent Note](implemented/process/2026-07-19-remove-generated-agent-note-index.md) owns the rationale. Delete an implemented record once its rationale can no longer guide future work.

## Classification

Each Agent Note belongs to one path-encoded class from the closed set in `scripts/agent-note-tree.ts`; the classification gate rejects other folders. Adding a class requires updating the canonical set and this section. See the [classification Agent Note](implemented/process/2026-06-20-agent-note-classification.md).

| Class | What it covers |
|---|---|
| `feature` | A new user- or model-facing capability. |
| `bug-fix` | Corrects a defect or closes a gap a postmortem surfaced. |
| `simplification` | Removes code, behavior, or surface area without adding a capability. |
| `architecture` | A structural decision about the **shipped source** — how packages relate, what the runtime vocabulary is. |
| `process` | Tooling, policy, or workflow **around** the code — gates, the package manager, vendoring — not runtime behavior. |
| `testing` | Test infrastructure and strategy. |

The `architecture` / `process` line: **architecture** is about the source we ship; **process** is the surrounding tooling and workflo
